leads.title: Remote work brought colleagues closer, a study of one company finds
leads.summary: Vanessa M. Conzon, a management professor at Boston College, followed staff at one professional services company before the pandemic and through 2024, as they moved from mostly working in the office to mostly working from home (four or five days a week). Her study, based on 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation, is peer-reviewed and due in an upcoming issue of the journal Organization Science. Contrary to her expectation, remote work made colleagues more open with each other, not less. In the office, people mainly saw each other as work colleagues and often hid personal circumstances. On video calls they glimpsed each other's children, pets and household noises, and got to know each other faster and more deeply, even people who had worked together for years. Psychological safety, the feeling of being able to speak openly without fear, appeared to improve. One worker said colleagues became 'less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives'. This openness led to more support: when one worker's father fell ill, a colleague took over their shared tasks so work did not stall. The author reports that the deeper collaboration did not come at the cost of getting work done, and the benefits appeared across different ages, family situations and genders. This is a qualitative study of a single company, so it does not prove the same happens everywhere. Published by The Conversation on 16 October 2026.

leads.title: Easy travel with a swivel seat
leads.summary: Two engineers from Bengaluru have made travel extremely easy for persons with disabilities. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre started a company named 'True Assistive Technology'. They have created a special swivel car seat named 'TurnPlus'. This seat rotates up to ninety degrees towards the car door. Because of this, passengers can be seated in the car without any trouble. Rashmi Sampat from Bengaluru lives with her sixteen-year-old daughter Deeksha. Deeksha is battling a disease called Spinal Muscular Atrophy. Earlier, seating Deeksha in the car was an exhausting task. With the help of this new seat, their family traveled from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari. They completed this long journey of one thousand kilometers very comfortably. The company has helped more than one thousand people so far. This technology is proving useful for patients with conditions like paralysis and Parkinson's.

leads.title: Youth initiative for plastic freedom
leads.summary: School students around the world are working to tackle the plastic problem. In a school in Singapore, seventy-two thousand plastic items were used every year. Students took part in the Unplastify Challenge and introduced reusable lunchboxes. With this great initiative, they won first place in this competition. This campaign is designed for teenagers aged fifteen to sixteen. Over the past eight years, three thousand students from twenty-five countries have joined it. Together, these children have helped prevent seventy-two tons of plastic waste. Students in Chile prepared a natural alternative to plastic glitter. In Costa Rica, natural loofah was used instead of plastic sponges. In Türkiye, students found an alternative to plastic gloves for health centers. The mindset of these young children is truly making the environment plastic-free.
